Zwolen Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Zwoleń, Poland

Demolished. Jews are first recorded in Zwoleń in the 16th century; by 1921, 3,787 Jews made up over half the town's population, and most were murdered at Treblinka in 1942. The cemetery likely dates to the late 16th or early 17th century, with its earliest documented references coming from a 1661 provincial inspection and a 1671 royal privilege. It held several wooden ohels and a mortuary by the 19th century. During the war it doubled as an execution and mass-burial site - roughly 100 to 200 victims of the 1942 deportation are buried there - and its stones were later used by German order to pave a road. Poland formally closed the cemetery in 1964 and built a park on the site; remaining tombstones were removed and buried. A 2014 archaeological survey by the 'From the Depths' Foundation uncovered destroyed matzevot underground, some of which are now held at the Regional Museum in Zwoleń.
